films.title: La Ballata Del Re Delle Api

seen_by.review:
first things first, the marketing team behind this and whoever created those trailers should all be fired, effective immediately.

now that that’s out of the way, ladies and gentlemen, we finally have the first minor masterpiece of the year. (I say this having not seen the invite yet)

it’s not perfect, and there are things I wanted more from, but overall this is brilliant. as a piece of satire, as a commentary, as a piece of art. it’s mature, intelligent, thought-provoking, emotional, hilarious, and manages to excel at the layers it keeps revealing along the way.

yes, Tom Cruise is impeccable. his best and most nuanced performance for sure. i had serious doubts after the trailers because i thought he was going to be way too over the top, but once you actually see the film, you understand why the performance is what it is. there are layers to what he’s doing that i would love to get into, but i genuinely can’t without ruining part of the experience.

and that’s actually the problem i’m having writing this review. i can barely talk about the film, because talking about it would immediately spoil it.

something happens that completely changes your perspective on what you’ve been watching. it changes the commentary, it reinvents the genre, and suddenly the structure itself becomes part of what the film is saying. i don’t even want to hint at what that means because you really should go into this blind. once you see it, you’ll understand why i’m being so vague and why it’s annoying me so much.

what i can talk about is what’s on the surface, and even there, this thing is firing on pretty much every cylinder.

right from the first three succession of shots, you know a master is speaking. but really, the whole thing is masterful. there’s such an economy to the shots, and such confidence in the blocking. something as simple as a character opening a door and momentarily hiding someone else in the frame… everything is minutely thought out. the production design, the costumes, the sound design… (especially the sound design!)
seeing that level of command over the craft is becoming increasingly rare and it’s truly a breath of fresh air.

and then there’s the monologue everybody is talking about. cruise is unbelievable, but the scene works this well because everything around him is operating at the same level. the direction, the camera work, the color palette of the room, the costumes of the extras, the editing, the performances. even the desaturated grading that I hated in the trailers ended up being one of the best part of the film because, again, there’s a reason for it that i cannot talk about.

but most importantly, the spectacular writing. the writing is excellent throughout, but stands out the most in that scene. it’s real and metaphorical. heartfelt and powerful while avoiding the generic cliches these types of monologues usually run into.

the whole scene is a painting. one of the best scenes of the year and probably one of the best scenes of the century.

the performances across the board are stellar. John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, even the secondary characters (especially the dad from gossip girl). the dramatic and comedic timing is overall impeccable, which is especially important because this is a film that speaks a lot. the excellent screenplay and the sharp dialogue are doing a lot of the work.
and it ends also perfectly. even the color of the font of the end credits is correct.

all that being said, there are things that don’t work quite as well. i wanted more from cruise and his daughter and that entire plot line. there are weaker characters (sandra huller), and i think there are places where the film could have gone slightly deeper emotionally.
I also didn’t have that overwhelming visceral reaction at the end that would push this into the very highest level for me. but these are details within something that is quite extraordinary.

go in blind. as blind as you can.

for now (from everything i’ve seen this year), this is easily the best film of 2026.

the haters have no idea what they’re talking about. and they can suck it.

indulges in its little meta gimmick too much, never completely committing to its own self-proclaimed powerful concept. But, at the end of the day, art will aways bring people together, even on the darkest of days - and it posits this well. Comes together nicely (after a very poor start), with a standout final moment that feels like a glimpse into a future not beyond the realms of possibility. Plemons is the man. I imagine this one will be ready for reclamation in 5 years or so.

Formally impressive, operating with some visual ideas that actually aid rather than come across as gimmicky obstacles. Thought I was going to hate it during the first 30 minutes: the coldness from the central relationship really seeped into the idea. I was getting virtually nothing from it. But, there’s a particular scene about an hour in where the meta-statement finally starts to hit. The final act is good stuff. Really liked the black & white bits, great lingering moments of angst.

films.title: Il Fuoco Che Ti Porti Dentro

seen_by.review: lives rebuilt from the rubble, an attempt to climb back to the surface while the devastation of what has been lost remains. Interweaves flashbacks in such a remarkable way: alternating between myth and real-world - there’s one scene in particular that is just so striking. The rare case of both bigger and better. I couldn't breathe during so many of its most thunderous moments; the destruction between Ghidorah and Godzilla is truly otherworldly. I had tears in my eyes during the entire final act. The quickest 135 minutes of all time.
3rd act flow state hit me like a magnitude 9 earthquake.

let’s get the negative out of the way. it mostly has the same flaws as the first one. the writing is still unbelievably subpar. no subtext, no poetry, just pure plot recital.
the acting gets pretty atrocious at times, especially from the two leads, and even more specifically from him. he either severely overacts or underacts.
all of that makes the emotional core of the film (the most important part) not believable, and actually quite weak.
so even though Min Tanaka stole the show, had the better sequences of the film, and gave arguably the best performance, the overall storytelling doesn’t work, which makes the whole highly forgettable.

now unto the positive. the fight sequences were fantastic. especially that midpoint battle with ghidorah and the pilots. we felt real stakes. real danger with fantastic pacing.
that filmmaker does not understand dramaturgy but goddamn does he understand scale!
every shot of these scenes, especially during the final confrontation, was almost a masterclass in action cinema. the editing perfectly matching the intensity of the score. the visual effects were astounding! the monsters don’t just look real. they have texture and grittiness on every one of their scale. all that stuff was edge of your seat filmmaking.
the ending scene was well done as well.

other than that, it’s pretty much a nothing burger, and I’m certainly not looking forward to the third volume.

absolute fucking banana land. what’re we even talking about?

Overly long galaxy-brained nonsense really.
Bay
-esque in lots of ways, and when it’s at its best, it’s absolutely blistering. It took me a second to lose myself in the universe as it deviated between the spills and thrills, but it wasn’t too long until I was fully locked in. Shockingly bizarre (complimentary), and the final chase made me feel as if I’d been injected with pure rocket fuel. Loses steam far too much to be an action great of this era, but its sheer lunacy can only be respected.

is it ridiculous? of course. but it completely owns how ridiculous it is. to the point where you can’t help but really enjoy it.

at some point, any suspension of disbelief just goes out the window and it just becomes hilarious. but I really think that’s the point. na hong-jin is a master and I think he knows exactly the kind of film he’s making.
the wailing and chaser were obviously much more serious films but still, he dabbled with the absurd. (especially in the wailing).
here he decides to swing into the territory of sci-fi, fantasy, action, comedy, all at once. and somehow it works a lot of the time.

sometimes it doesn’t. there are definitely moments where it pushes it too far, and some of the fights become so random and overly long that they took me out. for example the fight in the woods with michael fassbender went on for way too long, while the whole sequence with the car and the horse was nonsensically awesome.

but what i really loved was the mythology around all of it. the spaceship, the hunters going inside and exploring it, the design of everything, all the little details and easter eggs that make you feel like there’s an entire world here beyond what we’re seeing. even the exposition with the aliens at the end is so random and weird and awesome. I applaud this type of absurd world building.

the production design is incredible too. the sets are wonderful, the slow motion is effective, and even the CGI, which was questionable at the beginning, eventually becomes better and better. there’s something about the artificiality of the whole thing that feels completely intentional. almost like he’s playing with the language of the action genre itself and through his style, constantly commenting on it.

it’s fun and cool and I really didn’t expect it to take this many swings. not all of them land, but when they do, they really do.
justified alcoholic. can’t believe that ending had my eyes watering.

I often talk in my recent letterboxd reviews about how i struggled to connect with the stories being told or the characters being portrayed in most of the films I’ve recently seen. and sometimes i actually wondered whether I was the problem.
and then a film like this comes along, and i’m reminded that of course not, the film is the problem.

because when a filmmaker truly knows what he’s doing, when he’s a master of his craft like Koreeda is, he grabs you before you have time to blink, immerses you in his world, and doesn’t let go until the credits roll.

this is a return to form for him.
after one of the greatest debuts of all time with maborosi, and the sophomore major masterpiece that is still walking, the level of his work had somewhat declined over the years. but here, he’s back at the top of his game.

this is brilliant.

koreeda has this extraordinary ability to frame humans within nature, to bring the two together in compositions that are so colorful, so cohesive, and so moving.
and it’s not simply a matter of beautiful shots. it’s the choice of lenses, the grain, the colors of the costumes against the locations, the dreamlike editing… the artistry to it all is almost overwhelming.

and of course, this comes directly from the lineage of ozu, whose cinema shares so much of that sensitivity. koreeda is his greatest successor, and god is he worthy of that mantle!

the score is also wonderful, although not quite at the level of sakamoto, whose music brought something so unique to the other works of koreeda.
but beyond the visual artistry, the structure is lovely, and the relationship between the two protagonists is chef’s kiss. the whole thing is such a love letter to animation, to the creative process, but more broadly to friendship and the human endeavor of making art. and intertwined with all of that is this exploration of grief, expressed with subtlety and unbelievable poetry.

does it occasionally go a little overboard? sure. there are moments when i think a little more restraint would have made it even stronger.

I could have spent hours in that world crying, but alas, it had to end…

one of the best films of the year for sure.

PS: I have not seen the anime this is based on, and I’m glad I didn’t.

films.title: Ramayana - La Nascita Di Una Leggenda

seen_by.review:
before anyone asks, of course I saw this in hindi subtitled in english. I would never ever watch a live action film dubbed, I’m not a criminal. so you never need to ask again.

i thought the first part was really cool, and so was the last, but the middle section loses quite a bit of momentum. I think the film could have benefited from considerably more character development, both on the hero’s side and the villain’s.  emotionally, i never felt that invested.
the love story especially could have been much stronger. I kept thinking about the relationship between baahubali sr. and devasena in part 2, and how perfect that romance was.

visually, it was a blast. i actually liked the visual effects a lot, which surprised me considering how awful they were in the trailer. I also really liked being immersed in this mythological world and getting to know that culture a little better.

of course, this is only one part of a larger story. and even though i consider across the spider-verse a major masterpiece, despite it also being only one part of a movie, that film felt whole. I felt completely fulfilled by the end of it.
whereas here, it just sort of ends abruptly. even though I really liked that sequence with the eagle.

so yeah, I’d say average overall, especially when it comes to the storytelling and emotional investment (it’s no bahubali). but it had really awesome moments.

most people know, that apart from three billboards, I don’t really care for mcdonagh’s films. didn’t care for in bruges, and didn’t care for banshees… they’re fine films but that’s about it.

wild horse nine on the other hand… brilliant. and i’m the first surprised by just how good this is.

it’s profound and heartfelt, and somehow manages to speak about the geopolitical state of our world while remaining incredibly intimate and primarily focused on its characters and their plight.
on top of that, it’s hilarious! those first thirty minutes are among the funniest openings i’ve seen in a long time. as funny as the first thirty minutes of north by northwest!

malkovich is incredibly touching, and his chemistry with rockwell is wonderful. the way their relationship grows, and how the film gradually becomes this meditation on life and regret...
what do we think about when we’re approaching the end of our lives?

the words mcdonagh writes are unbelievably insightful, and malkovich delivers those words with incredible realness, no matter how dark it gets. it’s all completely absurd, and that’s exactly how it’s supposed to be.

a lovely surprise. and genuinely one of the best films of the year.

digger still on top tho.
